The clinical picture—progressive painless jaundice with intense pruritus, pale (acholic) stools, dark urine and weight loss—fits extrahepatic biliary obstruction. Abdominal ultrasound shows dilation of intra- and extrahepatic bile ducts with an anechoic cystic subhepatic structure; on exam there is a soft, non-tender, cystic RUQ mass consistent with a distended gallbladder (Courvoisier sign), which strongly suggests malignant obstruction of the distal bile duct rather than choledocholithiasis. Given the patient’s age, significant smoking history (a key risk factor), and constitutional weight loss, the most likely cause is a pancreatic head malignancy (adenocarcinoma) compressing the distal common bile duct and causing obstructive jaundice.

DIAGNOSIS: Obstructive jaundice due to pancreatic head adenocarcinoma (distal biliary obstruction).
